sentences.text: Mayors and other local political leaders could be given powers to oversee water companies under plans being considered by the government.
sentences.article_title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies

sentences.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham's plan is to create nine new regional bodies responsible for planning, setting objectives, and holding water companies to account.
sentences.article_title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies

sentences.text: The idea was a key recommendation of Sir John Cunliffe's Independent Water Commission published in June last year.
sentences.article_title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies

sentences.text: Improving the water industry has been a focus for Burnham since he took to power, as water customers in England and Wales continue to face steep bill hikes.
sentences.article_title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies

sentences.text: But there has been little detail of what that could look like, short of full nationalisation - until now.
sentences.article_title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies

sentences.text: Some ideas in the Cunliffe report were adopted by Sir Keir Starmer's government, however the recommendation for regional bodies was not.
sentences.article_title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies

sentences.text: While no final decision has been made, and the timings for any announcement have not been finalised, officials in the Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs are understood to be keen on the idea.

sentences.text: The regional bodies would be given powers to oversee elements of water companies' spending and hold bosses to account over bills and sewage discharges.
sentences.article_title: Mayors could be given powers to oversee water companies

sentences.text: After hearing from more than 130 witnesses, and considering 400 statements over six months, the Thirlwall Inquiry report was published earlier at Liverpool Town Hall.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: The inquiry began in September 2024, after Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others - one of whom she attempted to kill twice.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Below are the key findings from Lady Justice Thirlwall's report, which ran to more than 1,100 pages over three volumes.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: The first three deaths in June 2015 (babies A, C and D) were not viewed as a cluster of deaths, even though this was the annual number of deaths, concentrated into two weeks.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: The fourth death, (Baby E) in August 2015, was unexpected and therefore reviewed at a serious incident panel meeting attended by the medical director and director of nursing - but it was treated as a formality.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: "What is surprising is that no connection was made by any of the people involved to the earlier deaths," Thirlwall noted.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: By August of that year, the total of four deaths was the highest since 2008, and was to double by the end of the year.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Thirlwall found that if a doctor – named in the report as Dr ZA - had not disregarded the insulin test result for Baby F in August 2015 then there should have been safeguarding action.

sentences.text: She described a system of "dysfunctional management and governance".
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Lucy Letby was found to have falsified records Thirlwall found hospital bosses repeatedly failed in their duty of candour with parents, investigators and regulators.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: She added their behaviour was "high-handed, against all safeguarding principles, and foolhardy".
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Medical director Ian Harvey "sought to control the narrative",  and presented the case as he saw it.

sentences.text: He made sure that only documents that supported his case were seen, if necessary writing them himself.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: She also found that unit manager Eirian Powell's judgement "was affected by the view that Letby was a very good nurse".
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Thirwall found wider NHS failings played their part, with a tendency across the health service for management to become pre-occupied with avoiding blame and focusing on reputation management.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: She said there was still a "toxic negativity" that discouraged people within the NHS from speaking out, even though efforts had been made over the last decade to strengthen protections for whistleblowers.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Regulation was also found to be lacking.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: The Care Quality Commission (CQC) inspected the Countess of Chester in February 2016 but Letby carried on attacking babies until June of that year.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Key information was withheld from inspectors, but the regulator was criticised for not showing enough curiosity to look beyond what it was being told, even though the CQC had been warned by the inquiry into baby deaths at Morecambe Bay NHS Trust that it needed to take a tougher approach.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Thirlwall found their treatment to be "reprehensible", and said hospital executives used the risk of upsetting the parents as a convenient argument to justify not calling the police.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: The report found that "the way Letby's grievance and its consequences were handled was deplorable", adding that the investigating officer in charge "could bring neither independence nor objectivity to it".
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: The evidence of Alison Kelly and Ian Harvey was found to be "factually inaccurate and misleading", and the chair of the governance panel, Annette Weatherly, was "unfair in her approach", having initially described the allegations against Letby as a "witch hunt".

sentences.text: Police were called into the hospital in 2017.

sentences.text: She had falsified records and one infant in her care had been found covered in their own faeces.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: She was also found to have been repeatedly untruthful in her dealings with friends and colleagues, and was noted by patients to have been "inappropriate" and "callous" in her manner.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: Thirlwall made 17 recommendations in her report, which ran to over 1,100 pages over three volumes.
sentences.article_title: What are the key findings from the Thirlwall inquiry?

sentences.text: She said that cots and incubators in neonatal units should be fitted with baby monitors, and access to insulin - which Letby was convicted of administering to two of the babies she killed - should be controlled by either biometric data or CCTV monitoring.

sentences.text: She also said a "suspicion of deliberate harm" policy, which outlines the steps to be taken by managers when suspicions are raised, needed to be created, and that NHS staff should be contractually obligated to follow the policy and other safeguarding guidance.

sentences.text: The US defence department's inspector general says the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump who has repeatedly denied the US is facing shortages.

sentences.text: The BBC's defence correspondent explains what the US announcement means The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Washington has given away little in its announcement.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: So what could this weapon be, and what is the wider picture like for military developments in space?
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Who else could have similar weaponry?
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Space has been a militarised domain since the start of the space age - in the late 1960s, the Soviet Union deployed weapons up there.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: The Istrebitel Sputnikov (IS; Satellite Destroyer) programme was made up of satellites that were designed to release projectiles that detonated, releasing shrapnel into the path of another (usually American) satellite.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Nowadays, advanced militaries deploy satellites in space for a range of purposes, including reconnaissance, secure communications, detecting missile launches and providing precise location information for targeted strikes.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: As warfare becomes more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Some types of space weaponry could create a lot of debris and destruction Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless." Bowen also would not rule out a riskier and more disruptive type of weaponry, which could create debris and destruction.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: A type of "close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well." As to whether rivals such as Russia and China have similar weaponry already in orbit, is difficult to tell.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "If we're looking towards China and Russia, they have both displayed activity," Juliana Suess, a former research fellow at RUSI and researcher at the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (German Institute for International and Security Affairs), told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "For example, with Russia, we've seen some activity that hints at being a co-orbital weapons test.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: So we saw something that might indicate that they shot a projectile as a test in orbit.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: In a later BBC interview, Bowen was dismissive of China's reaction to the US announcement which warned against an arms race in space, describing it as "the pot calling the kettle black".
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "If you're already an expert... you know how hollow those words are coming from the Russian and Chinese governments," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "The United States, Russia and China and also India have all developed different kinds of anti-satellite or counter-space weapons, and Russia and China have put a lot of technologies in space which have a lot of weapons potential," he added.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: In fact in the past 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "Theoretically, these RPO [satellites]can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Bowen added that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit." This, he said, could be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: However, some types of space weaponry also have the potential to create huge amounts of space junk.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Dr Mark Hilborne, a specialist in space security and weaponisation at King's College,  said direct ascent anti-satellite missile tests, such as one carried out by China in 2007, leave a great deal of debris in orbit for a very long time.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Suess said debris from that test was still in orbit and still dangerous.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "It doesn't have to be a sort of huge piece of metal to do any damage, it can be a tiny piece of plastic, given the velocity that we're talking about in orbit," she said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Thornton said that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike [satellites] in low Earth orbit.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: They also have ASAT [air-launched antisatellite] missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Only if it was happening on the ground as well.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "What could happen in space is not something that would happen in isolation, really," Bowen said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "Nothing could happen, or something could." This video can not be played Watch: US Space Force Guardians spring into action during training exercise Given that weapons for use in space have been around for so long, why did the US announcement come when it did?

sentences.text: Experts agree that it's not a major development as such, more a political signal.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Bowen suggested that it could be a response to Chinese developments.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: "China has modernised its military forces over the past 30 years," he said.
sentences.article_title: What weapon could the US have put into space?

sentences.text: Thornton said that, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, because it has so few satellites, unlike China and the US.

sentences.text: It would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring satellites designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers," he said.

sentences.text: African wild dogs are among Africa's rarest predators, with only about 6,000 remaining in the wild.
sentences.article_title: Wild dogs record 2,500-mile trek across Zambia in search of a mate

sentences.text: They live in highly social packs, hunt together and are known for their vast roaming in search of new territory and breeding opportunities with other packs.
sentences.article_title: Wild dogs record 2,500-mile trek across Zambia in search of a mate

sentences.text: They cannot breed within the pack they are born into, so they either wait and may eventually inherit their pack, or set off at the age of two or three in search of a mate.

sentences.text: The brothers covered about 260 miles in a straight line over the course of eight months, but travelled nearly 10 times that overall while crossing through a broken-up landscape.

sentences.text: These sorts of journeys are known as dispersals - travelling one way in search of a mate, which is a behaviour distinct from migrations, where animals move back and forth with the seasons in search of food or habitat.

sentences.text: Globally, caribou undertake the longest single land migrations of any animal - travelling 839 miles in a round trip, while grey wolves have been recorded travelling more than 4,350 miles over a year.

sentences.text: Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.

sentences.text: The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.
sentences.article_title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline

sentences.text: The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran.
sentences.article_title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline

sentences.text: This video can not be played Watch: Ukraine's post office innovation helps isolated communities Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: But Smelyansky is no military commander.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: "If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: The key is to be as agile as you can." Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated." There are many risks.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: But if they call ahead, information could leak.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: "Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming." If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver." Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: "It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.

sentences.text: A file photo of a Ukrposhta post office damaged during strikes in Kyiv in April We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.

sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us.
sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.article_title: Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire

sentences.text: Scientists searched for the inclusion of the Gaelic words for oyster or oysters – eisir, eisirein and eisirean – and oyster habitats like sandy banks or tidal causeways in place names around Scotland's coast.

sentences.text: They then found an oyster bed that had not been previously documented, as well as confirming oysters could have been present at other sites on Mull and Islay.

sentences.text: Native oysters were once abundant in coastal European waters, including Scotland, but now only remnant populations are known to remain due to overharvesting and disease.

sentences.article_title: Lost oyster beds rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language

sentences.text: Dr Anna McGregor, an expert in coastal ecology and a lecturer at the University of Glasgow , had the original idea of locating oysters through traditional place-names, then applying scientific techniques to confirm oyster presence within them.
sentences.article_title: Lost oyster beds rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language

sentences.text: She explained: "This is a really exciting outcome, for a project that started off looking for the historic distribution of oysters along the West Coast.
sentences.article_title: Lost oyster beds rediscovered thanks to Gaelic and Scots language

sentences.text: Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: The government wants digital ID apps under its scheme to work together so customers do not need to use different apps in different venues.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: It also wants the services to work offline and accessible even without mobile data or a Wi-Fi connection.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: In future, the digital proof of age scheme could be extended to cover tobacco and vapes.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: But digital rights campaigners have said such measures could lead to the exclusion of some groups.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: Jasleen Chaggar of Big Brother Watch said while having multiple ways to prove your identity was helpful, the Government should ensure that digital ID did not become effectively mandatory "as it would shut out millions of people".
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: "Many people have legitimate reasons for relying on physical ID, whether out of choice, privacy and security concerns, or because they lack the digital skills or means to use digital ID," she said.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: "The Government should expressly prohibit businesses from requiring digital IDs for age checks without offering reasonable alternatives," she added.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: The new rules come after a wider digital ID programme promoted by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer proved controversial , and was later abandoned by Andy Burnham.
sentences.article_title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

sentences.text: The ban comes just weeks after an unrelated protest in Dover when anti-migrant demonstrators covered their faces with balaclavas Offenders wearing balaclavas to hide their identity cause "substantial" problems in Nottingham, a police chief has said as a new ban came into force in the city.

sentences.text: The proposals were announced last year by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood Trade unions are putting pressure on the government to soften proposed changes to immigration rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: If the plans are approved, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for permanent residence, rather than five years, while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: The proposals were announced last year by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood , who has kept the same role under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Delegates at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) backed a motion calling for any changes affecting workers already in the UK to be withdrawn.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: A government spokesperson said ministers had received 200,000 responses to a consultation on the proposals, which was launched under Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, and they were carefully considering them.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Giving evidence to MPs on the Commons Home Affairs Committee on Tuesday, Mahmood said technical details for her new migration system were now being worked on and she expected to announce policy later this year.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: "We're trying to strike the right balance between our responsibilities to people who have come here to work, our recognition of the failures we inherited as a government, and also our need to do right by the people who are already here, who pay for the systems that we all rely on," she said.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Under the government's proposals the standard wait to qualify for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain, would increase to 10 years.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: People who arrived on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait, while those who relied on benefits for more than 12 months would have to wait 20 years.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Indefinite leave to remain gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: The changes would not apply to people who have already obtained settlement but would cover people already living in the UK, including those who had been expecting to get permanent residence in the coming months.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Some Labour MPs have also criticised plans for the changes to apply to migrants already in the UK.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Earlier this year, when she was a backbench MP and not a government minister, Angela Rayner, herself a former care worker, labelled the proposals "un-British" .
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Rayner, who has since been appointed housing secretary by Burnham, warned that "moving the goalposts undermines our sense of fair play".
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: At the time, Burnham, who was still Greater Manchester mayor, said he understood where Rayner was "coming from" and that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Don't change rules for migrants already in UK, Labour MPs tell Mahmood Reform plans to scrap indefinite leave to remain for migrants The UK's biggest union, Unison, called on delegates to agree they were "alarmed at sweeping attacks on migrant workers which render them second-class citizens in the UK".
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: Unison head Andrea Egan told the BBC: "I can't understand why a Labour government have brought these proposals in.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: "These are workers that have come from overseas to support a social care system, a health system that was absolutely buckling under stress.
sentences.article_title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules

sentences.text: "They answered that call on a contract with the government... work for 5 years and you'll get the right to remain.

sentences.text: Fire crews hosed down an overheating tank in Los Angeles in May An industrial nightmare was brewing south of Los Angeles.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: In late May, a chemical storage tank with more than 7,000 gallons of toxic material began heating up – fast.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: The tank belonged to GKN Aerospace, a company that supplies parts to the aviation industry, including aircraft windows.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: As the temperature inside the shiny metal storage vessel rose, workers realised they had a problem.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: The tank was at risk of exploding, potentially showering nearby neighbourhoods with methyl methacrylate (MMA), a skin and lung-irritating , external compound used in plastics production.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: The tank's temperature reached 100F (38C) – though possibly went higher - 100F was simply the maximum reading , external on the temperature gauge inside.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: More than 50,000 residents of Garden Grove city were evacuated and fire crews began hosing down the tank in a bid to cool it.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: At one point, the vessel "actually bulged" according to the local fire chief.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Thankfully, no explosion occurred.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Months later, in August, GKN and local authorities announced a $100m (£74m) programme , external to compensate residents evacuated during the incident.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: But production of aircraft windows at the site, which had been halted, is still not fully restored.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Very few companies make aircraft windows This has sent a minor shockwave through the aircraft manufacturing industry because GKN is one of surprisingly few companies, anywhere in the world, that make aircraft windows – highly engineered, safety-critical parts for planes.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Production at GKN's Garden Grove facility currently remains hobbled, at roughly 50% of normal, according to public statements , external by its UK parent company Melrose Industries.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: The aim is to have full production restored by 28 September.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: GKN declined an interview with the BBC.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "They're one of only a handful of suppliers – less than a handful, really – of critical windows," says Marisa Garcia, an aviation industry analyst.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "We are supporting our supplier," a spokesman adds.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: An Airbus spokeswoman says, "We are closely monitoring and are seeing positive progress toward a return to normal." It comes at a time when airlines "can't get new aircraft fast enough," says Mike Stengel of AeroDynamic Advisory, a consultancy.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "They're holding on to aircraft for longer." Even though there are just a few aircraft window-manufacturing firms in existence, it's hard for new competitors to emerge because of how regulated the industry is, adds Stengel.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "It can take time to pivot to a new supplier." This leads to a "balancing act" between plane-makers and the firms they rely on for various parts, Stengel says.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Windows start with a sheet of acrylic To find out what goes into the making of an aircraft window, I spoke to Jean-Eric Vermont, general manager of French company Saint-Gobain Aerospace.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "We focus mostly on commercial aircraft, regional aircraft and helicopters," he says.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Vermont declines, though, to say how much market share his company has in aircraft windows – or transparencies, as they are known in the trade.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: The oval-shaped windows in the cabin, next to passengers' seats, are typically made of plastic-based materials, says Vermont.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "You start from a sheet of acrylic," he explains.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "Then you cut to size, [to] give the shape." A Saint-Gobain spokesman confirmed to the BBC that the company does not store or process MMA like GKN, but rather purchases sheets of polymerised MMA, or acrylic.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Aircraft manufacturers are increasingly ordering larger cabin windows, says Vermont, in order to offer passengers a wider view of the world outside.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: It's a selling point but it requires additional testing to ascertain whether the bigger windows hold up as well as the smaller ones.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Saint-Gobain tests its windows by exposing them to pressures many times what would be normal on an aircraft flying at altitude.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: These acrylic-based cabin windows are usually made out of two layers or plies, and Saint-Gobain also performs tests to confirm whether the window will survive even if one of those plies gets damaged.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: As aircraft windows get bigger, they get harder to manufacture Cockpit windows, Vermont says, are "totally different".
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: They are generally made of glass, which is chemically reinforced by adding potassium to it.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: This involves swapping smaller sodium ions for larger potassium ions, which helps to fill out the molecular structure of the glass, meaning that when it cools during production, it compresses into an extra strong, tight formation as it cools.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Some of the latest aircraft feature cockpit windows that are also curved, to make the plane more streamlined, which improves fuel efficiency.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: But curved cockpit windows are challenging to make – the slightest distortion or defect is clearly visible to the pilot.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: Quality control checks are used to ensure no such impediments exist in the final product.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "Typically, if you go through a hailstorm or if you hit a large enough bird, the external ply will crack," says Vermont.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "The cockpit window is designed for that." A London to Londonderry flight was recently affected by a cracked cockpit window .
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: While a mid-air emergency was declared, the plane landed safely.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "There can be [such] cases," says Vermont, though he adds that Saint-Gobain's windows have not been involved in any recently.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "You're obviously dealing with a surface that is interfacing with two very different environments," says Stengel.
sentences.article_title: The extreme engineering of aircraft windows

sentences.text: "That's why these are more highly-engineered products." Will self-flying planes transform the skies?

sentences.text: US President Donald Trump has said fears about the safety of artificial intelligence (AI) are a "hoax", as he criticised calls to have more guardrails in place for the fast-moving technology.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: It comes after Jack Clark, co-founder of AI giant Anthropic, told the BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Clark's comments followed warnings about the risks the technology poses to humanity that have been raised in recent days by several executives and staff at leading AI firms.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Those concerns triggered a selloff in tech firms' shares as investors weighed the impact of a potential slowdown in the multi-billion dollar development of AI.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: In a series of social media posts, the US president compared warnings about AI to the "Global Warming Scam" which, he said, was "being perpetrated by the Radical Left Dumocrats".
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Trump also called himself "the Hoax Buster", likening concerns about the safety of the technology to what he called "the RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX".
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: The only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president, said Trump.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: In another post he wrote: "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!" Chinese state media said experts had warned that "Washington's growing anxiety over China's rapid AI development appears to be increasingly distorting its policy priorities".
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: "They know that China has become a strong competitor in AI, and worry that if the US slows down development or tightens regulation, China could catch up even faster," Xin Qiang, a professor of American Studies at Fudan University, told the Global Times.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Clark, who is one of Anthropic's seven founders, said earlier on Monday that a way of shutting off AI software completely if it gets too dangerous was something society "might want to eventually pass rules around".
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: He added that "most labs have different ways of being able to pull the plug", including Anthropic, but said lawmakers may need to enforce having one.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Microsoft AI's chief executive Mustafa Suleyman told business news channel CNBC that it had been working on the new guidance for months and had decided to publish it now due to the current debate around the technology.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: In an indication of how concerns over the technology have been thrust into the spotlight, two high-profile figures on opposite sides of US politics are set to appear at the same event calling for a re-evaluation of AI policy.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Former Trump chief strategist Steve Bannon and veteran progressive Senator Bernie Sanders are due to speak at the "Pro-Human Assembly" in Washington on Tuesday.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: According to its website the gathering "aims to define a shared vision and articulate a better, more human-centric path for AI development".
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Sanders told BBC's Newsnight last week that "we have got to do something immediately to stop the uncontrolled growth of AI".
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: "You've got the existential threat of the possibility of humanity being wiped out," he said.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: The debate over the potential dangers posed by the technology intensified in recent days after a post by Jacob Coxon , a researcher who left Anthropic over concerns AI could wipe out humanity, went viral.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he thought the possibility of AI causing human extinction "within the next decade" was more than 10%.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored, as the company has done before, though some have questioned the motivations behind this.
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: Amodei also said that any action to rein in AI should be done "without sacrificing commercial advantage".
sentences.article_title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

sentences.text: The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, have also said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.

sentences.text: Chinese firms dominate battery production Europe has taken some big swings in the battery industry in recent years and has made a couple of high-profile misses.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Both Sweden's Northvolt , external and Norway's Morrow , external filed for bankruptcy and there are fears in Europe that the continent has missed another technology shift.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: With more transport and industry switching from fossil fuels to electricity, batteries are likely to be a growth business.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: But the length of time required to bring new products to market, coupled with brutal competition, especially from China, means taking a substantial risk.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Could the answer lie at an almost unimaginably small scale?
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: An increasing number of investors and researchers think so.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: A single nanometre is one-billionth of a metre, but it's at that level that some of the most consequential work is being done.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "If you can make this work, it touches so many industries [but] it's a risky business," says Christian Rood, chief executive of Dutch tech firm LeydenJar.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Named after a 18th century precursor to electric cells, LeydenJar uses a technique known as plasma deposition to make a lighter, more efficient anode – an essential component of all batteries.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Silicon is a highly effective and cheap material to use in anodes, but pure silicon expands and contracts as the battery operates and is recharged, which causes it to crack.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: However, using plasma deposition, LeydenJar can - layer by tiny layer - make an ultra-thin pure silicon foil which resists cracking, allowing a significant increase in battery life, charging speed, and energy density (up to 50%, according to LeydenJar).
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "Where normally a pure silicon anode would fall apart, [this] remains stable, so it was a very wonderful invention," says Rood.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "We address the bottleneck in the battery." LeydenJar's tech could mean better batteries Commercial-scale production will start at the end of 2026, but it has taken 10 years to get to this point – the very definition of the time and investment required for so-called Deep Tech innovations.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: It's no coincidence that LeydenJar's factory is in the Dutch city of Eindhoven - home to ASML and other important players in the computer chip industry.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "A lot of people talk theoretically about ecosystems; I can tell you this is one of our sources of competitive advantage," Rood says.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "It's really the crossover from semiconductors to batteries that makes us different - once you've demonstrated the principle in the lab, industrialization requires you to work with the semiconductor technology and suppliers.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "That means a lot of risk, but also a lot of opportunity in terms of patenting, in terms of securing your whole intellectual property.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: And that's much more difficult to do in the US or in China." Across the Netherlands and Europe more widely there are multiple smaller Deep Tech start-ups looking to develop nanotechnology in the battery market.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: One of those is Powall, a start-up in the Dutch city of Delft that is developing commercial-scale equipment for nanocoating the powders that are the raw materials of today's batteries.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Again, the scale is tiny, and once again the technique was born in the semiconductor industry.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Individual powder granules are measured in micrometres, the coatings in nanometres - they are applied using a technique known as atomic layer deposition.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Roderik Colen, CEO of Powall, tells me that the system offers multiple opportunities to adjust and improve the performance of today's batteries.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "Your battery works less well than before after using it thousands of times - that degrading or aging can be slowed down when you're using a nanocoating," Colen explains.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "You can have an exciting new material with a higher capacity or fast charging, all these novel developments.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: They typically have one element which is very good, but they suffer on the durability side." And that means they will never be a commercial product.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "That's where we then come in, to give them the protective coating to effectively enable these new materials." The powders and the coating are carried by gas and brought together in a chemical reaction.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: It is, says Colen, a precise but flexible process which can be almost endlessly adapted.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "You have great accuracy in how thick you want to have it.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: And that makes a difference in performance." Powall is developing nanocoating for battery components Neither LeydenJar nor Powall are trying to build an entire battery, and both have commercial relationships with customers in Asia.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: But Christian Rood of LeydenJar says companies like his can fortify Europe's position in what has become a global contest.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "The easy comparison is with semiconductors, where there's really a race for the best chip technology.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "[Dutch tech giant] ASML is not producing chips; it focuses on a critical step in the production of chips, and in that way, has a seat at the table when it comes to the whole semiconductor battle.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "This is our ambition as well – to have a position where our battery anode is so unique that we have an important position in the supply chain." So, how do these ambitions play into Europe's goals in the battery industry?
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Alexander Brown is a senior analyst at the Berlin-based independent think-tank the Mercator Institute for China Studies (Merics).
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "I think having one part of the supply chain based in Europe is great and if that can be a very advanced technological part, which offers the opportunity for high margins, that's fantastic," Brown tells me.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: But he cautions that while "there can be collaboration as well as competition at the same time", China in particular will continue to work to reduce its dependence on other regions.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "China is working very hard to develop local alternatives for technologies, including these niche technologies.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "It's no secret that China would love to replace ASML - they're working very hard to do that, and it's not unforeseeable that they will achieve that goal eventually.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "So, I think Europe has traditional strengths in developing very exquisite high-quality products, which can find markets all over the world.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "But I also think it's important for that not to be the only strategy [from the continent's policy makers]." The challenges of working in such a specialised field are not only technological.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: LeydenJar has already reached commercial scale, but Rood says that raising funds within Europe is not always easy.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "There is sufficient financing in Europe, but the risk attitude is quite different than in Asia and in the US," says Rood.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "That means for a company like us that you have to work with different sources of funding at the same time," Rood explains.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: He lists government grants, debt financing, help from the European Investment Bank and investors willing to buy a share of the business.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "They set a lot of challenging conditions, and they all want to do their own due diligence.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: It's hard work," Rood says.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: Powall's Colen says Europe, and the Netherlands in particular, is an "innovation powerhouse", and battery technology offers a chance for the continent to make an impact, if the appetite for the risk is there.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: "It's a relatively young industry where factories are being built left, right and centre.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: They're searching for the right tech.
sentences.article_title: Can Europe recharge its battery industry?

sentences.text: So that's where you can play a big role, because the volumes are huge." Perhaps Europe's place in that business lies not in building huge battery gigafactories, but at the other end of the scale altogether.

sentences.text: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage pictured during the party's annual party conference earlier this month The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: The government is planning to tighten residency rules for people giving money to political parties, to ensure that those making significant donations live in the UK.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But it is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to £100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published, , external the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons , external that cap would be £100,000 per year.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: They have both now returned to the UK.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would be legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: "Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Ah, today, I pointed out.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: This video can not be played Farage: Donations to Reform '100% compliant with the law today' We don't know, because Reform won't tell us, precisely when the two men relocated to the UK.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Nor do we know, because the government hasn't decided yet, what relocating - residency - would look like legally.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Would it be being on the electoral roll at a UK address?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Would it be being resident in the UK for tax purposes?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: In other words the hurdles they plan, while still ill-defined, look like they might be quite high - and folk in government, publicly and privately, are leaning into making that point.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Farage picked a scrap with them in his interview with me, and the government is hitting back.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Do Delo and Harborne clear them, and if they don't, for how long could that delay Reform getting hold of their vast sums of money?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: The Reform UK leader has threatened that a Reform government would cut off party funding from the trades unions if the government went ahead with trying to limit his capacity to raise money from these two donors.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Labour received £5m from affiliated unions last year and £12m the year before, in 2024, the year of the last general election.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today' Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: So, there are loads of questions that tumble towards us after these donations.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Should there be a limit on the proportion of a party's funding that can come from one individual?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Should there be a limit on what donors based in the UK can give per year, as well as a cap on donations from Brits abroad?
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: The General Secretary of the Unite union has suggested a domestic cap somewhere between £500,000 and £1m a year.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Some argue this would compel parties to find their funding via lots of small donations rather than fewer giant ones.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: But it could also prompt some to call for state funding of political parties – ie taxpayers picking up the tab – which may not prove wildly popular.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: Then there is the question of spending limits, in addition to donation limits, between elections on the top of the existing limits that do apply just before elections.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: If I am leaving you with the impression that these donations to Reform, and in particular their scale, are transforming the debates at Westminster about politics and money, well - they are.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: And yes, all of the political parties are aware of their own narrow, self interest in all of this - as well as their own sense of the wider good.
sentences.article_title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet

sentences.text: A cross-party group of MPs and peers has identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI), arguing existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth.
sentences.article_title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights

sentences.text: The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.
sentences.article_title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights

sentences.text: "Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," said Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel.
sentences.article_title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights

sentences.text: Labour education minister Georgia Gould said AI was creating opportunities but that it was critical the government was "responding to those risks" posed by the technology.
sentences.article_title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights

sentences.text: In a summary of its 100-page report, the JCHR argued AI has been responsible for numerous abuses of human rights, citing examples including the use of AI to create sexualised images of women and girls, and scanning people's faces without their consent.
sentences.article_title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights

sentences.text: The JCHR has advocated for the creation of a "single, independent AI oversight body... on a statutory basis", saying the current legal framework is "fragmented and difficult to navigate", "leaving gaps in protection".
sentences.article_title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights

sentences.text: The report goes on to call for "more demanding obligations for higher risk AI systems and models" at all stages of the "AI lifecycle".
sentences.article_title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights

sentences.text: It continues: "Some uses of AI should be prohibited outright because they are incompatible with human rights.
sentences.article_title: MPs and Lords call for new law to address AI threat to human rights

sentences.text: What is clear is that at present we are unprepared to deal with its consequences however potentially dire they may be." The JCHR's 12 members are drawn from both Houses of Parliament and they currently include MPs and peers from the Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat parties.
